content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Congress passed the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) in 1980 out of concern that uniform regulations disproportionately burden small firms.\1\ The Office of Advocacy (Advocacy) is responsible for monitoring agencies' compliance with the RFA and educates rule-writing staff on the effect their rules would have on small businesses. Advocacy seeks to find targeted solutions that are less burdensome, and in Fiscal Year 2023 (FY 2023), their efforts resulted in more than $90 million in estimated regulatory costs savings for small businesses.\2\
\1\Stuart Shapiro & Deanna Moran, The Checkered History of Regulatory Reform, 19 N.Y.U. J. Legis. & Pub. Pol'y 141, 153-54 (2016) (describing hearings leading up to passage of the RFA).
\2\Off. of Advoc., U.S. Small Bus. Admin., Report on the Regulatory Flexibility Act: Fiscal Year 2023 (2024), https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/RFA-FY23_ final.pdf.
Concerns have been raised by the Coalition for Sensible Safeguards and other organizations that the RFA has become a tool for large businesses to obstruct the regulatory process. To that end, the ``Prove It Act of 2025'' would give the biggest companies a powerful new tool to use against regulations that protect our health, environment, and safety, and cause further harm to the very small entities it purports to help. Cumbersome New Process Giving Powerful Trade Groups Too Much Influence
First and foremost, the bill creates an unworkable quasi-judicial process within Advocacy for reviewing agencies' certification that a regulation would not have a ``significant economic effect on a significant number of small entities (SEISNSE).'' Unlike the original RFA, which only allows small entities to seek judicial review, the ``Prove It Act of 2025'' ``would allow an ``organization representing the interests of small entities'' to file a petition for review with the Chief Counsel of Advocacy. This new process would let powerful trade associations like the U.S. Chamber of Commerce petition the SBA to review a certification as long as the organization can claim to represent some small entities affected by the underlying rule. Moreover, the bill would allow these organizations to challenge the agencies' certifications without identifying which small businesses they represent or how those small businesses would be harmed by the rules they are challenging.
Once a petition is filed, the Chief Counsel would have 10 days to determine if the petition warrants a full review. If the Chief Counsel determines that a full review is required, the Chief Counsel has 30 more days to conduct the review and publish the results. This new process would result in additional meetings with the representatives of small entities, agencies, Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), and Advocacy. Multiple and duplicative petitions could be received on the same rule, resulting in numerous reviews and meetings. Indirect Economic Effect Cost Estimates
The bill would also require agencies to include indirect economic effects of rules in their regulatory flexibility analyses, which can be burdensome, impracticable, and counterproductive. Under current law, the RFA requires agencies to take into consideration the direct impact on small entities and try to minimize the direct impact while achieving the same goal. Indirect costs are significantly more difficult to estimate, and agencies do not always have that information available to them, nor do they have control over minimizing them. Unreviewable Discretion Granted to the Chief Counsel
In addition to creating a new process, the bill gives the Chief Counsel unreviewable discretion to sanction the agency promulgating the rule by making the final rule inapplicable to small entities upon the finding that the agency failed to assist the Chief Counsel. With 99 percent of businesses being designated as small, the bill would allow Advocacy to essentially gut a regulation.
The Chief Counsel must also track agency completion of mandatory reviews of existing rules every 10 years. It requires agencies to also conduct retrospective reviews based on the indirect costs identified in the initial analysis. This provision doesn't make sense because agencies may have changed the rules significantly between proposed and final rule stages, meaning the indirect costs identified in the proposed stage may not be applicable to the final rule, let alone 10 years after the final rule has taken effect. To that end, the provision is unworkable.
If the Chief Counsel finds that an agency failed to conduct a required review of a rule, the Chief Counsel could suspend operation of the rule, meaning it wouldn't apply to anyone or any business. This provision creates another layer of regulatory review, which would essentially allow Advocacy to freeze a regulation until an agency review is conducted and then possibly reinstate the rule--causing undue uncertainty to small businesses.
In the 118th Congress, Advocacy shared with Democratic Committee staff that small businesses need certainty in the rule-making process and requiring small businesses to come into compliance with a rule or regulation only to remove it from the books would be onerous in and of itself. Advocacy further stated, ``rules are integrated into one another, and they have a much broader impact in terms of who it affects, further contributing to the uncertainty in the rulemaking process, particularly for small businesses that procure with the federal government.'' CBO Score
Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates the bill would increase administrative costs for most agencies, including Advocacy. Accordingly, CBO reported that H.R. 7198, identical legislation introduced in the previous Congress, would increase direct spending for independent agencies by $10 million, reduce revenues by $7 million over the 2025-2034 period, and increase spending by $35 million over the 2025-2029 period, subject to the availability of appropriated funds.\3\ In sum, the enactment of this bill would result in significant costs to the taxpayer, and it would likely not result in any meaningful reduction of the burdensome requirements to small businesses.
\3\Cong. Budget Off., H.R. 7198, Prove It Act of 2024, Cost Estimate (Dec. 2, 2024), https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61042.
Moreover, by opening the door for well-resourced trade associations to challenge virtually any rule, the bill could end up requiring the Chief Counsel to review agencies' RFA compliance for many of the thousands of rules issued each year, to say nothing of agencies' periodic reviews of existing rules. That would do little to help small businesses but would help powerful companies with money to hire well-connected lobbyists.
The Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that the four agencies they reviewed to assess compliance with the RFA generally met statutory requirements, but almost half hadn't received training since 2003. GAO made six recommendations, including one requiring the Office of Advocacy to develop and implement procedures to provide training on RFA compliance, including identifying the agencies most in need of training.\4\
\4\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., Regulatory Flexibility Act: Improved Policies for Analysis and Training Could Enhance Compliance (Apr. 10, 2025), https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-25-106950.
Committee Democrats offered four commonsense amendments to improve the bill, but Republicans rejected them all.
Ms. Goodlander offered an amendment to require organizations to list the name, address, telephone number, and email of the small businesses they are filing a petition on behalf of with Advocacy. The commonsense amendment would close a loophole in the bill that allows powerful trade associations to exploit the process by filing a petition without naming the small business they are representing. Committee Democrats supported this good government amendment that would bring transparency and accountability to the process. The Majority rejected this amendment on the grounds that listing the name, address, phone number, and email of the small business the National Federation of Business (NFIB) and Chamber of Commerce file a petition on behalf of would be an unnecessary administrative burden.
Mr. McGarvey offered an amendment that would carve out an exemption for any rules that the agency finds would have a substantial beneficial impact on veterans. He stated, the Prove-It Act is the ``same unworkable policy that would empower the country's biggest corporations to paralyze all federal rulemaking under the guise of protecting small businesses.'' He offered the amendment to protect veterans from the damage of the Prove-It Act, given all Republican cuts they are facing to programs like, Medicaid, health care, and SNAP. The Republicans argued that the amendment would create and exemption that would undermine transparency and accountability and defeated it.
Ranking Member Velazquez offered an amendment requiring Advocacy to train rule-writing staff at agencies on how to comply with the Regulatory Flexibility Act, at least once every four years, and require agencies to submit a report on the retrospective review of rules. The Prove-It Act disregards the meaningful progress that agencies have been making to examine the impact a new rule would have on small businesses. Rather than create an adversarial process between Advocacy and the agencies under the Prove-It Act, the amendment would foster a more constructive working relationship that would lead to more success. The Republicans rejected this amendment on the grounds that it would create ``an uncertain and burdensome environment.'' It is ironic because the the Prove-It Act would require small businesses to come into compliance with a rule only to take it off the books ten years later, if a retrospective review was not conducted in a timely manner and then put it back on the books if the retrospective review was conducted. Small businesses need clear, consistent rules of the road, not chaos. Without a solid argument against the amendment, the Republicans relied on the argument that it will result in more ``bureaucratic red tape.'' It is important to note, that the Prove-It Act would establish a whole new bureaucratic process filled with new analytical and procedural requirements, making the rulemaking process significantly more complex.
Mr. Olszewski offered an amendment to carve out an exemption for any rules that the agency finds would have a substantial beneficial impact on workforce development programs and rural small business owners. He pointed out the problems with the Prove-It Act and stated his amendment would strengthen our workforce and uplift small rural businesses. The Republicans rejected this amendment based on the flawed assumption that it would result in fraud. I countered that the fraud Mr. Finstad was referring to started under the first Trump Administration.
In conclusion, Committee Democrats could not support the Prove-It Act, which creates an unworkable bureaucratic process, and allows powerful companies to exploit rulemakings that benefit small businesses, and protect the health and safety of all Americans.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
